In [[mathematics]], the '''trigonometric [[moment problem]]''' is formulated as follows: given a sequence <math>\{c_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}_{0}}</math>, does there exist a [[Distribution function (measure theory)|distribution function]] <math>\sigma</math> on the interval <math>[0,2\pi]</math> such that:{{sfn | Geronimus | 1946}}{{sfn|Akhiezer|1965|pp=180-181}}
<math display="block">c_k = \frac{1}{2 \pi}\int_0 ^{2 \pi} e^{-ik\theta}\,d \sigma(\theta),</math>
with <math>c_{-k} = \overline{c}_k</math> for <math>k \geq 1</math>. An affirmative answer to the problem means that  <math>\{c_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{N}_{0}}</math> are the [[Fourier series#Fourier-Stieltjes series|Fourier-Stieltjes coefficients]] for some (consequently positive) unique [[Radon measure]] <math>\mu</math> on <math>[0,2\pi]</math> as distribution function.{{sfn|Edwards|1982|pp=72-73}}{{sfn|Zygmund|2002|p=11}}{{sfn|Katznelson |2004|p=40}}{{sfn|Schmüdgen|2017|p=260}}

In case the sequence is finite, i.e., <math>\{c_k\}_{k = 0}^{n < \infty}</math>, it is referred to as the '''truncated trigonometric moment problem'''.{{sfn|Schmüdgen|2017|pp=257,261}}

== Characterization ==

The trigonometric moment problem is solvable, that is, <math>\{c_k\}_{k=0}^{n}</math> is a sequence of Fourier coefficients, if and only if the {{math |(''n'' + 1) &times; (''n'' + 1)}} [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] [[Toeplitz matrix]]
<math display="block">
T =
\left(\begin{matrix}
c_0       & c_1           & \cdots   & c_n     \\
c_{-1} & c_0           & \cdots   & c_{n-1} \\
\vdots         & \vdots             & \ddots   & \vdots       \\
c_{-n} & c_{-n+1} & \cdots   & c_0     \\
\end{matrix}\right)</math> with <math>c_{-k}=\overline{c_{k}}</math> for <math>k \geq 1</math>,
is [[Positive-semidefinite matrix|positive semi-definite]].{{sfn|Schmüdgen|2017|page=260}}

The "only if" part of the claims can be verified by a direct calculation. We sketch an argument for the converse. The positive semidefinite matrix <math>T</math> defines a [[sesquilinear]] product on <math>\mathbb{C}^{n+1}</math>, resulting in a [[Hilbert space]]
<math display="block">(\mathcal{H}, \langle \;,\; \rangle)</math>
of dimensional at most {{math|''n'' + 1}}. The Toeplitz structure of <math>T</math> means that a "truncated" shift is a [[partial isometry]] on <math>\mathcal{H}</math>. More specifically, let <math>\{e_0,\dotsc,e_n\}</math> be the standard basis of <math>\mathbb{C}^{n+1}</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{E}</math> and <math>\mathcal{F}</math> be subspaces generated by the [[equivalence class]]es <math>\{[e_0],\dotsc,[e_{n-1}]\}</math> respectively <math>\{[e_1],\dotsc,[e_{n}]\}</math>. Define an operator
<math display="block">V: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow \mathcal{F}</math>
by
<math display="block">V[e_k] = [e_{k+1}] \quad \mbox{for} \quad k = 0 \ldots n-1.</math>
Since
<math display="block">\langle V[e_j], V[e_k] \rangle = \langle [e_{j+1}], [e_{k+1}] \rangle = T_{j+1, k+1} = T_{j, k} = \langle [e_{j}], [e_{k}] \rangle,</math>
<math>V</math> can be extended to a partial isometry acting on all of <math>\mathcal{H}</math>. Take a minimal [[unitary operator|unitary]] extension <math>U</math> of <math>V</math>, on a possibly larger space (this always exists). According to the [[spectral theorem]],{{sfn|Simon|2005|pp=26,42}}{{sfn|Katznelson |2004|pp=38-45}} there exists a Borel measure <math>m</math> on the [[Circle group|unit circle]] <math>\mathbb{T}</math> such that for all integer {{math|''k''}}
<math display="block">\langle (U^*)^k [ e_ {n+1} ], [ e_ {n+1} ] \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{T}} z^{k} dm .</math>
For <math>k = 0,\dotsc,n</math>, the left hand side is
<math display="block">
\langle (U^*)^k [ e_ {n+1} ], [ e_ {n+1} ] \rangle
= \langle (V^*)^k [ e_ {n+1} ],  [ e_{n+1} ] \rangle
= \langle [e_{n+1-k}], [ e_{n+1} ] \rangle
= T_{n+1, n+1-k}
= c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}.
</math>
As such, there is a <math>j</math>-[[atomic measure]] <math>m</math> on <math>\mathbb{T}</math>, with <math>j \leq 2n + 1 < \infty </math> (i.e. the set is finite), such that{{sfn|Schmüdgen|2017|page=261}}
<math display="block">
c_k = \int_{\mathbb{T}} z^{-k} dm
= \int_{\mathbb{T}} \bar{z}^k dm,
</math>
which is equivalent to
<math display="block"> c_k = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0 ^{2 \pi} e^{-ik\theta} d\mu(\theta).</math>

for some suitable measure <math>\mu</math>.

=== Parametrization of solutions ===
{{see also|Spectrum (functional analysis)#Classification of points in the spectrum}}
The above discussion shows that the truncated trigonometric moment problem has infinitely many solutions if the Toeplitz matrix <math>T</math> is invertible.{{sfn|Curto|Fialkow|1991|p=634}}{{sfn|Iokhvidov|1982|pp=97-98}}
In that case, the solutions to the problem are in bijective correspondence with minimal unitary extensions of the [[partial isometry]] <math>V</math>.
